newsitem.title: USA: Deep Blue makes chess history by beating Kasparov.
newsitem.headline: Deep Blue makes chess history by beating Kasparov.

text.p: The supercomputer Deep Blue made chess history on Sunday when it defeated Garry Kasparov for an overall victory in their six-game re-match, the first time a computer has triumphed over a reigning world champion in a classical chess match.

The Russian grandmaster collapsed in the decisive game, resigning with the black pieces after only 19 moves and just over an hour at the board. He walked away from the playing room looking stunned, waving his arms in distress.
"I have to apologise for today's performance," Kasparov told a news conference. "I had no real energy to fight."

The match score of 3-1/2 points to 2-1/2 points was achieved with wins by the computer system in games two and six and three draws. The 34-year-old Kasparov won the first game on May 3. One point is awarded for a win and a 1/2 point for a draw.

On Sunday the IBM system sacrificed a knight in the opening after an apparent error by the world champion. Ultimately, the computer's position was unbeatable and after exchanging his queen and a pawn for a rook, a bishop and a knight, Kasparov resigned.
Deep Blue team manager Chung-Jen Tan praised Kasparov.
"Garry has a brilliant mind and he understands where computers can take us," Tan told reporters.

Deep Blue's match win was the first by a chess-playing computer in a traditional format in which games can last as long as seven hours. The team of computer scientists and a full-time grandmaster consultant collected the winner's prize of $700,000. Kasparov, considered the best player in the history of the ancient game, was awarded $400,000.

The scientist's victory with the massive calculating machine was revenge for Deep Blue's loss to Kasparov over six games in Philadelphia in February 1996, when Kasparov won three games, drew two and lost one.

The experts said the moves played by both players in an opening known as the Caro-Kann defence had previously been played in grandmaster games and undoubtedly were programmed into Deep Blue's huge database by the scientists who created it.

Kasparov had to put aside his fear of the IBM-calculating machine in order to attempt winning the game and the re-match. In five games over eight days, an improved and modified Deep Blue has shaken the confidence of the player considered to be the best in the history of the ancient game.

"I have to be afraid because I can outcalculate any player in the world easily but I cannot outcalculate this machine," Kasparov said after Saturday's fifth game, in which the system forced him to agree to a draw following some artful endgame strategy.

Deep Blue is an IBM RS/6000 SP parallel processor with specialised microchips for chess that can examine hundreds of millions of possible moves per second. Since their first match in Philadelphia in 1996, the machine's speed has been doubled and it has been infused with more chess knowledge. Kasparov won the Philadelphia match.

The event is part chess match and part research project to help build computers that can make complex, simultaneous calculations for applications such as weather forecasting, air traffic control and molecular dynamics, according to IBM.

Kasparov easily won the first game on May 3, but then the system played brilliantly in the second game, the turning point psychologically and emotionally for the champion. In an oversight rarely seen in grandmaster play and never before from Kasparov, he needlessly resigned in a drawn position.

The error was confirmed in post-game analysis and Kasparov said it affected his performance in the next two games, both draws. But Deep Blue deserved the draw Saturday when it fought the endgame in a manner that won the admiration of the experts and Kasparov himself.
